publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (American Psychological Association)
vintage: 205 widowed spouses (Changing Lives of Older Couples) followed from before the loss to 6 and 18 months after
title: Resilience to loss and chronic grief: A prospective study from preloss to 18-months postloss
authors: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman, Tweed, Haring, Sonnega, Carr and Nesse (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, doi 10.1037/0022-3514.83.5.1150
universe: Older adults whose spouse died, interviewed before the death and at 6 and 18 months after
geography: Detroit Standardized Metropolitan Statistical Area, United States
limits: Spousal loss in old age only, so the resilient share is lower than the 65.7% pooled across all potential traumas (trauma-trajectories-2018.json); the band the town is held to stays the pooled one, and this lower figure is the reason that band may be generous for bereavement alone. Symptom trajectories, not actions.
quote: As anticipated, most of the sample (n = 185; 90.2%) were captured by five conceptually relevant patterns: common grief (n = 22; 10.7%); chronic grief (n = 32; 15.6%); resilient (n = 94; 45.9%); chronic depression (n = 16; 7.8%); and depressed-improved (n = 21; 10.2%).
use: A caution beside the pooled band in scripts/research/people-year.ts: for bereavement alone, resilience is the most frequent pattern but not the majority.
